answer: History, not a forecast. A savings bond held 20 years is guaranteed to reach at least double its price, about 3.53% a year. Rolling 3-month T-bills for 20 years, starting any month from 1934 to 2006 (873 starts), ended above double in 52.3% of starts (median multiple 2.097; range 1.129 to 4.612). Today's doubling terms apply to bonds issued from May 2005; for the 856 earlier start months (98.1% of all starts) we apply them as if they had existed then. It was a matter of era: starts from 1950 to 1989 ended above double in 93.1% of months, starts from 1990 on in only 5.0%. The latest full stretch, Sep 2006 to Aug 2026, turned money into 1.378 times. In the 17 start months when the guarantee really existed (May 2005 to Sep 2006), rolled T-bills ended at 1.378 to 1.388 times the money; none reached double. Double itself is not inflation-proof: it kept up with consumer prices over 20 years in 58.7% of start months (median buying power 107.3% of the original). In Aug 2026 the 3-month bill rate was 3.72%.
guess: With T-bills paying 3.72% against the bond's 3.53% doubling rate, most savers would guess rolling T-bills easily beats a bond that 'only' doubles in 20 years.
changesDecision: Today's T-bill rate is only the first of 80 three-month rates the saver would get over 20 years: the roll beat double in nearly every start from 1950 to 1989 and fell short in nearly every start from 1990 on. For 87.6% of the starts from 1990 on, the average bill rate over the next 20 years was below the rate in the start month. Double bought less than the original money in 41.3% of start months; the worst, starting in January 1966, bought 58.0% of what the money bought at the start. That reframes the choice as a known result in dollars versus a bet on 20 years of short-term rates; no forecast of rates is made.

assumptions: The doubling guarantee is applied to every historical start as if it had existed then; it applies to bonds issued from May 2005, and earlier bonds had other terms.

T-bill returns use the monthly average 3-month rate divided by 12 each month (discount-basis rate, not converted to investment yield), compounded monthly; transaction costs and gaps between rolls are ignored.
Taxes are ignored: T-bill interest is federally taxed each year, while savings bond interest is federally tax-deferred until redemption; both are exempt from state income tax.
Savings bonds cashed before 20 years earn only their stated fixed rate (and lose 3 months of interest before 5 years); the comparison assumes a full 20-year hold.
Annual purchase limits on savings bonds are ignored.
limits: History, not a forecast. Starts from 1934 to 1949 never ended above double. The data from 1934 to 2026 hold only 4 separate 20-year periods; the 873 overlapping windows are not 873 independent results. Ignoring taxes favors T-bills relative to tax-deferred savings bonds for most savers.
